title: What to make of China’s new air facility in Laos
gist: China has announced a Chinese-funded pilot training centre at Ban Keun Airport near Vientiane whose ~2,000m runway can land PLA fighters and Y-20B transports but not long-range bombers. Together with Ream in Cambodia it outflanks Vietnam, reflects Laos' deep economic dependence on China, and any runway extension or exclusive-use upgrade would sharpen threat perceptions in Canberra and Washington.

insights.claim: China has announced a Chinese-funded Joint Support and Training Centre and China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy at Ban Keun Airport, about 50 km north of Vientiane, officially to train Laos Air Force pilots and 'not directed against any third party'.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Marks a new Chinese military footprint in mainland Southeast Asia that may function as a de facto base.
insights.quote: The Chinese official statement added that the training centre “is not directed against any third party”.
insights.locator: The Joint Support and Training Centre

insights.claim: Satellite imagery shows the Ban Keun runway is about 2,000 metres long, enough to land most PLA fighter jets such as the J-10 and J-11 and Y-20B transport aircraft, but too short for long-range PLA bombers that need closer to 3,000 metres.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Runway length is the key observable indicator of whether the site escalates into a strategic power-projection base.
insights.quote: the runway is about 2,000 metres (Opens in new window) long, sufficient to land most People’s Liberation Army (PLA) fighter jets

insights.claim: The Ban Keun airfield was previously Lima Site 44, used by the US military and the CIA during the Vietnam War mainly for resupply and transporting ground forces.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Historical precedent shows the site's strategic value for inland force projection.
insights.locator: The same airfield was previously known

insights.claim: It is unclear how China would use the Laos airbase in peacetime, but one suggestion is that it could let the PLA air force preposition aircraft for joint exercises with Thailand, shortening travel distances.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Peacetime use for exercises would normalise PLA presence in mainland Southeast Asia.
insights.locator: However, it is unclear how China

insights.claim: Some commentators argue Ban Keun and Cambodia's Ream Naval Base together would let China project force over both inland and maritime domains, while other analysts stress the two are fundamentally different and that the Laos air site is a novel addition to China's overseas military operations.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Analysts disagree on whether China is building an integrated regional basing network.

insights.claim: Laos may have been a more appealing partner for China than Cambodia because the Hun Manet government recently restored military exercises with the United States and allowed the US Navy to dock vessels at Ream.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Cambodia's hedging toward Washington is shifting where Beijing places military assets.
insights.quote: The Hun Manet government in Phnom Penh recently restored (Opens in new window) military exercises with the United States
insights.locator: According to one analyst cited by Rudy Lu

insights.claim: China provided roughly two-thirds of Laos' foreign direct investment in 2024 and owns the largest share of the country's debt, making Laos dependent on China.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Debt leverage gives Beijing potential to convert economic dependence into military access.
insights.quote: Laos has become dependent on China, which provided roughly two-thirds (Opens in new window) of Laos’ foreign direct investment in 2024
insights.locator: Laos has become dependent on China

insights.claim: When Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith visited Beijing in June 2026, the two sides pledged to expand defence ties and Xi Jinping proposed an annual '3+3' dialogue, signalling the priority the Chinese Communist Party places on the relationship.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Institutionalised party-to-party and defence ties indicate a durable China-Laos alignment.

insights.claim: With a military facility in Laos plus Ream naval base in Cambodia, Beijing has effectively executed an end run around Vietnam's air and maritime flanks, and no other regional country is as directly exposed as Vietnam.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Heightened Vietnamese threat perception could accelerate Hanoi's defence spending and alignment with the US and partners.
insights.quote: Beijing has effectively pulled off an end run around Hanoi’s air and maritime flanks. No other country in the region is as directly exposed as Vietnam.

insights.claim: The long-term impact of Ban Keun depends on how the PLA uses it, whether Beijing leverages Vientiane's dependence to gain an exclusive base, and whether the runway is lengthened to land long-range bombers such as the H-6; any of these would draw scrutiny beyond Southeast Asia and sharpen threat perceptions in Canberra and Washington.
insights.speaker: Hunter Marston
insights.so_what: Watch for runway extension as a trigger for escalation in US and Australian defence posture.
insights.quote: Any of those changes would draw greater scrutiny from beyond Southeast Asia and sharpen threat perceptions in Canberra and Washington.
